blocks.text: She clings to the false and the wrong as firmly as she proclaims the true. [II, 855] Nor do we need to run to the farthest Indians to learn the nature of the swan; although it is common in Holland and Britain, all the Dutch and British nevertheless deny that they have observed any such thing in the swan. Of the same stamp is what Clytus, the disciple of Aristotle, writes in Athenaeus, book 14, about the bird meleagris: Ἔστι δὲ ἄστοργον πρὸς τὰ ἔκγονα τὸ ὄρνεον, καὶ ὀλιγωρεῖ τῶν νεωτέρων, ὥστε ἀνάγκη τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἐπιμελεῖσθαι αὐτῶν [Esti de astorgon pros ta ekgona to orneon, kai oligōrei tōn neōterōn, hōste anankē tois hiereusin epimeleisthai autōn]; This animal has little affection for its offspring, and neglects its chicks so much that the priests must take care of them. For by the name meleagris Clytus describes the hen which we call the Indian or the Barbary hen, and the ancients the Numidian: both scarcely yield to the common hen in natural φιλοστοργίᾳ [philostorgia] toward their chicks. Nor do certain Arabs more truly lay the same charge against الحباري [al-ḥubārā] alhubara, that is, the bustard. Alkazuinius: قالوا ما في الطيور اشد منه بلها يترك بيضها [qālū mā fī al-ṭuyūr ashadd minhu balahan yatruku bayḍahā] [col. 251] وتحضن بيض غيرها وفي المثل كل شي يحب ولده حتي الحباري [wa-taḥḍunu bayḍ ghayrihā wa-fī al-mathal kull shay yuḥibbu waladahu ḥattā al-ḥubārā] They say that no bird is more foolish than it, since it abandons its own eggs and sits on those of others. Hence the proverb: Every animal loves its young except the bustard. But Damir, who has written more about the bustard than anyone else I know of, at least clears the female of so shameful a charge in these words: قال عثمان رضي الله عنه كل شي يحب ولده حتي الحباري خصها بالذكر لانها يضرب بها المثل في الحمق وهي علي حمقها تحب ولدها فتطعمها وتعلمها الطيران كغيرها من الحيوان [qāla ʿUthmān raḍiya Allāh ʿanhu kull shay yuḥibbu waladahu ḥattā al-ḥubārā khaṣṣahā bi-al-dhikr li-annahā yuḍrabu bihā al-mathal fī al-ḥumq wa-hiya ʿalā ḥumqihā tuḥibbu waladahā fa-tuṭʿimuhā wa-tuʿallimuhā al-ṭayarān ka-ghayrihā min al-ḥayawān] Othman, to whom may God be gracious, said that every animal loves its offspring except the bustard. But this properly applies to the male. For although the common proverb imputes folly to the female, yet for all her folly she loves her chicks, feeds them and teaches them to fly, just like the other animals. Someone must also have deceived Jerome when he wrote of the dove on Os. VII.: The other birds hasten to protect their chicks even at the peril of their own life, etc. The dove alone does not grieve for its chicks when they are taken away, and does not seek them. Surely there is no one who does not know that the affection of doves, both toward their chicks and toward their mates, is most tender. Male and female sit on the eggs ἐκ διαδοχῆς [ek diadochēs], that is, by turns; and in like manner they συνθερμαίνουσι [synthermainousi], warm together, the hatched chicks. And if the female returns too sluggishly after the pains of laying, the male calls her back to the nest with a light chastisement. They share the care of ψωμίζειν [psōmizein] the chicks, putting predigested food into their mouths; and when taken away from the nest, however great the distance, they return to it out of love for their offspring. Hence it has come about that some have used doves as messengers, sending them back with a note attached to the town where they had sat on eggs or chicks. Hence Oppian, book 3 [Cyneget.], verse 115.
[II, 856] Πῶς δ᾽ ἄρ ἐν οἰωνοῖσι ποθὴν ἀλίαστον ἔχουσιν Ὧν τεκέων φῆναί τε, βαρύφθογγοί τε πέλειαι. [Pōs d' ar en oiōnoisi pothēn aliaston echousin / Hōn tekeōn phēnai te, barypthongoi te peleiai.]
